summary:
Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment, and enforcement is active rather than dormant. Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression, and enforcement of both provisions falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.

The scale of the current campaign is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, so the sweep is national in character rather than confined to one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released only after sentence reduction.

Human Rights Watch recorded at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months in 2016, all convicted under Article 230. Detainees interviewed in those cases reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police, which places physical abuse by the security services inside the ordinary arrest process rather than outside it.

Tunisia pledged to the United Nations in 2017 to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay law itself, so the commitment changed examination practice without decriminalising anything. A visitor should not read that pledge as a change in exposure to prosecution.

Legal gender recognition is unsettled and frequently refused. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, weighing contradictory lower-court judgements, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent; the question remains unresolved below the Court of Cassation, which makes recognition a court-by-court gamble. Cairo 52 records that gaps persist in legal gender recognition generally.

Custody carries documented identity risk. The Intersection Association reported in November 2024 that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity from the point of detention onward and a source of continuous suffering inside the prison system. A trans visitor who is detained should expect documents and hearings to use a name and gender marker they do not recognise.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern in Tunisia resembles other states that retain colonial-era sodomy statutes alongside broad public-morality offences, but the 2024–2025 sweep is unusually documented in scale: 84 arrests across four cities in four months, with mass sentencing and a failed appeal. Comparable jurisdictions in the region have not produced conviction figures of that density in the same period.

The gap between international commitment and domestic law is a recurring feature of the Tunisian record. The 2017 pledge to the United Nations on forced anal testing sits alongside retention of Article 230 and continued reliance on public indecency provisions, so treaty engagement has not translated into statutory change.

Gender-expression exposure runs through morality and debauchery provisions rather than through a dedicated anti-trans statute, which means police discretion at the point of arrest does much of the work. Trans women appear in the arrest data in disproportionate numbers relative to their share of the population.
localsOnly:
Residents face a legal gender recognition process that is decided case by case with no settled precedent. The April 2023 refusal by the Tunis Court of First Instance and the contradictory lower-court judgements it examined, including case No. 12304/2018, mean an application can succeed or fail depending on the bench, and the issue is not resolved above the Court of Cassation.

Transgender women inside the prison system are recorded under former names and birth gender across detention records, arrest paperwork and court hearings, according to the Intersection Association's November 2024 reporting. The association describes this as continuous suffering and discrimination embedded in custodial procedure rather than isolated incidents.

Domestic advocacy and litigation are the routes through which recognition and custody conditions are contested, and the absence of consistent precedent means each case sets a data point rather than a rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry screening, visa conditions, airport document checks or border treatment of trans travellers, so exposure at the point of entry is unresolved rather than assessed.

The inventory does not establish whether Tunisia has hate-crime or anti-discrimination provisions covering gender identity, nor whether any such provision is enforced; protection machinery beyond the criminal law is not sourced here.

Whether Article 226 bis has been used against gender expression in any specific prosecution with a known sentence is not documented in these sources; its application to gender expression is asserted in the record without a cited case.

Current prison population figures for transgender detainees, and any post-2024 change to legal gender recognition practice, are not sourced and remain open.
